intent: understand WagerProof model and market analysis
title: How a WagerProof analysis separates model, market, and result
description: A transparent walkthrough of the WagerProof research contract: market definition, live price, model estimate, disagreement, context, grading, and limitations.
dek: A model estimate, a market price, and the final result answer different questions. WagerProof is most useful when those layers remain visible instead of being collapsed into one pick label.
author: chris-habib

hero.alt: A blueprint flow from market definition to model estimate, comparison, context, and grading
hero.caption: AI-assisted editorial illustration of the research sequence. It is not a product screenshot or model-performance claim.

disclosure: This is a first-party explanation of the WagerProof product contract, not publication of proprietary model code or an independent validation. No backtest, win rate, or accuracy statistic is claimed here.
verdict: A WagerProof analysis begins with a precisely defined market and live price, adds a versioned model estimate, displays the difference, and keeps context and grading visible. The difference is a research prompt. It is not proof that the market is wrong or that the outcome is certain.

faqs.question: Does a larger WagerProof model-market gap guarantee a winning outcome?
faqs.answer: No. The gap is the difference between a model estimate and a current market-derived probability. It can reflect a useful disagreement, stale data, model error, price movement, or uncertainty. Every outcome can still lose.

faqs.question: How should WagerProof model estimates be evaluated?
faqs.answer: Preserve the model version, information cutoff, market, price, and every forecast. Review calibration, price quality, and results across comparable samples without deleting losses or changing the rule after the event.

faqs.question: Why does WagerProof show graded records?
faqs.answer: A complete graded history lets a reader inspect wins, losses, pushes, units, and selection behavior rather than seeing only successful examples. A record still needs sample-size, price, and rule-change context.
